Triggers.value: Feeling physically restrained or held down

Threat.value: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Memory.value: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with the simultaneously severe, poorly processed trauma-memory profile implied by 'Full Sensory Reliving' and 'Olfactory Recall'. Those latter items suggest intrusive sensory re-experiencing, while very easy verbal access points in the opposite direction and is hard to reconcile in the same profile without additional context.

The Threat node is not coherent internally: 'Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating' is a non-threat/cognitive impairment item, whereas the other threat items are specific hypervigilant danger-monitoring states ('Waking Alert', 'Startle to Movement'). This makes the Threat selections thematically inconsistent.

Cross-node coherence is weak around 'Triggers: Being Followed'. That trigger implies a persecutory/social-tracking danger theme, but the rest of the profile centers more on restraint, safety checking, startle, and sensory reliving, without corresponding appraisals or memories about pursuit/tracking. It feels insufficiently integrated with the rest of the formulation.

'Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Going Out' is not well linked to the selected trigger/threat pattern. The profile emphasizes tiredness, restraint sensations, night-time safety checking, and movement-related startle, but not a clear outside/public-space threat theme. Avoiding going out therefore appears mismatched to the rest of the selected content.

vignette:
Mila, a 19-year-old European American woman, had been living in a small apartment near the studio where she worked as a dancer when the event that changed everything occurred. One evening she was on her way home after rehearsal, still in costume layers under her coat and feeling drained from a long day, when the city street around her was thrown into chaos by a sudden man-made disaster nearby. In the confusion that followed, she was caught in a crush of people and held in place against her will, with strangers pressing in around her and no clear way to move. The experience was not just terrifying in the moment; it left her with a vivid, bodily memory of being physically restrained and unable to get free while the world around her felt dangerous and out of control. Afterward, she found that the memory could return with startling force, and when it did it felt completely real across all her senses at once. She could be standing in her kitchen or sitting in the studio and suddenly be back there, with the same pressure on her body, the same panic, and even the same smells rising up as if they were in the air around her again. At times she would catch a scent that seemed to belong to that night, and it would pull her back so quickly that she could not separate then from now.

In the weeks that followed, Mila started organizing her days around keeping herself from being caught off guard again. She stopped going out except when she had to, and even then she planned routes carefully, kept to familiar streets, and hurried from one place to the next. The outside world had begun to feel like a place where danger could approach from anywhere, and she was especially uneasy when she felt tired or exhausted, because that was when her guard seemed to slip and the memories or fears came in harder. At home, she sometimes covered her face with her hands when she heard sudden noise in the hallway or when someone came up too close too quickly, as if hiding would make her less visible and less vulnerable. She also gave up pleasant activities she used to enjoy, including casual outings with friends and unplanned time after work, because she could not relax into them; any moment of enjoyment seemed risky if it left her exposed or unprepared. Over time, this narrowed her life. Invitations were declined, she became harder to reach, and the easy social rhythm that had once come with being a young dancer began to disappear.

Mila described a persistent sense that what happened to her was deeply unfair and that nothing had been done about it. She spoke with frustration about how the event had been treated by others, as though there was no proper acknowledgment of what she had endured. That sense of injustice sat beside a growing conviction that she no longer belonged anywhere. Even at the studio, among people she had known for years, she felt as though she was on the edge of everyone else's life rather than part of it. She remained committed to dance, but she found that concentrating during rehearsals had become difficult. Choreography she had learned quickly before now seemed harder to hold in mind, and she would lose her place if too much was happening around her. Unexpected movement nearby made her react as if she were in danger; a dancer crossing suddenly behind her, a teacher stepping into her line of sight, even a door banging open could send a jolt through her body. At night she often woke to check whether she was safe, scanning her room and listening for signs that something was wrong before she could let herself settle again.

When she tried to talk about the disaster, Mila often said she knew what happened but could not find the words to describe it. The facts were there, but they did not come out in a neat sequence; what came instead was a stopping, a tightening, and then a retreat into silence. The combination of vivid bodily memories, constant alertness, and a life increasingly shaped by avoidance had left her exhausted and isolated by the time she came for help. She sought treatment because she was tired of feeling trapped in the same fear, of waking up checking the room, of flinching at movement, and of shrinking her world until it no longer felt like her own. What she most hoped for was to be able to move through her days without bracing for danger, and what frightened her most was that if she thought too much about the event, she would not be able to handle it.
